chapter: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
title: George Buck, Jazzology and the albums in the works
summary: She ran into Buck, producer of Fat Cat's early albums, and has made two more for release, including a Spencer Clark session.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well you work allot down there.
Yeah, well I ran into George Buck, who is the producer for Jazzology and it was George

S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC.

Buck who produced those first albums of Fat Cat. But now George Buck is doing his own thing. There seems to have been a split between the two of them. And I have some friends who live down in Southern Pines, North Carolina who used to be located up in Manchester, New Hampshire, and I used to go up to New Hampshire and do a private thing for them with guys like Herb Hall and Cheatham, Herman Autry Doc and those guys. So anyway, Joe Robertson is is name and he was to promote these concerts up there to raise funds for Andover, the school up there because he had kids in there. So he moved down to Southern Pines and he retired and moved on to Southern Pines to live permanently. And so I kept in touch with him and said, get something going down there in North Carolina. He's an ex-trombone player. He made his living in the linen service but he liked to play the trombone. So sure enough I got a call from him and he said, 'I got something going, I got a gig down here but I can't get a piano player.' I said, 'Well you got to get a piano player.' So it just so happened that Art Holder was going to be down that way playing in Columbia, South Carolina and he was going to make a recording for George Buck. So he got Art
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

up here in Southern Pines for Joe Robertson, a double feature, Art Hodes and Maxine Sullivan. And while I was down there I got stranded because it snowed in New York and I couldn't get home. George Buck came up to Southern Pines and he agreed to make a recording so we stopped on the way and made an album which is recently out called, "We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye", and that of course was with Art Ho[de] and a group of musicians from down that way. And . . .
And there are two more in the works?

Yes, two more in the works. I made two at that time and it was - the other album was just made with a trio. I happened to run into - George Buck asked me if I knew Ike Isaacs, a bass player who was married at one time to Carmen McRae, and a very popular jazz bass player and he happened to be my cousin. So we contacted Ike and I got a trio together and we made an album the next day. I don't know when that's going to be released but the early part of this year I went down to Wispering Pines with Doc Cheatham and Red Richards and Herb Hall and we made another album while we

were down there. So I guess that will be released eventually. We don't exactly when but we're hoping soon. And just recently I was down in Wilmington, North Carolina and did a jazz festival down there with a group of musicians. They got the North Carolina Jazz Society down there and they put on this three day festival. It was quite fabulously done. You haven't got the list in front of you but they had Jack Lesberg, Bud Freeman, Milt Hinton, Doc Cheatham, Herb Hall, Cliff Leeman, Dick Welsted, and some of the musicians that are better known in the South. But most of these guys . . .

Spencer Clark was on my recording of 'We Just Couldn't Say Goodbye'. But there are alot of jazz societies scattered all over the United States. I worked out in Minneapolis with Herb Hall. There is the Hall Brothers out there. Real traditional dixieland jazz. And this is where I ran into a man by the name of Bill Drake. He's in the paper somewhere and he likes to play the drums. And most of these traditional jazz bands are made up of guys who just want to play - they want to play dixieland. So that's the crowd I seem
